title: Learning the Dose Manifold: A Latent Diffusion Framework for Volumetric Dose Prediction in Automated Radiotherapy Treatment Planning

paper.title: Learning the Dose Manifold: A Latent Diffusion Framework for Volumetric Dose Prediction in Automated Radiotherapy Treatment Planning
paper.abstract: Abstract Automated treatment planning (ATP) aims to reduce the unwarranted inter-planner variability of manual planning, while improving treatment quality and efficiency. Most ATP pipelines rely on the prediction of the achievable three-dimensional dose distribution for a given anatomy and the subsequent optimization of machine parameters to reproduce it. Diffusion-based methods are largely slice-wise due to the high dimensionality of radiotherapy data, and assume a one-to-one mapping between anatomy and optimal dose despite the multi-objective nature of treatment planning. They are evaluated on their ability to match reference doses and rarely on their integration in ATP frameworks. We present LaDose, a latent diffusion framework for fully volumetric dose prediction. An autoencoder learned on dose distributions, trained so that perturbed latents decode to plausible doses, compresses dose maps 128-fold and enables 3D diffusion on a single GPU. Prescription values are represented as exact scalar vectors that bypass the image encoder, avoiding resampling and latent compression. Multiscale classifier-free guidance allows for the modulation of clinical trade-offs at inference, without retraining or additional labeled data. On 900 clinically delivered head-and-neck volumetric modulated arc therapy plans from five centers, LaDose reached a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy (1.4–1.8% of the prescription) and was the only one of six frameworks free of systematic bias with respect to the reference distribution. Guidance scales acted predictably on target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing. Integrated with direct aperture optimization, the pipeline generated plans in 15.2 minutes; in a blinded review, senior clinicians rated 14 of 15 plans acceptable without editing.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Radiotherapy is indicated in the management of an estimated 52.3% of cancer patients ( Delaney et al., 2005 ) . Treatment planning is a highly complex and time-consuming inverse optimization process, aiming to deliver a prescribed dose to the planning target volume (PTV), while sparing surrounding organs at risk (OARs). Traditionally, dosimetrists manually adjust beam parameters and structure-specific objectives to iteratively refine the plan until it satisfies protocol constraints. As the trade-offs achievable for a given anatomy are not known a priori, this process is a manual search whose stopping point is determined by the time available and by the planner’s experience ( Hussein et al., 2018 ) . As a consequence, manual planning introduces wide inter-planner variability, including in the compliance with the constraints that determine clinical acceptability ( Nelms et al., 2012 ) . Part of this variability reflects different institutional protocols and clinician preferences, which an automated replacement must take into account explicitly. The remainder stems from limited planning time and expertise, and is the variability that automated treatment planning (ATP) aims to remove through standardization, improving plan quality and consistency while reducing planning time ( Momin et al., 2021 ) . Modern ATP pipelines often rely on direct aperture optimization with dose-mimicking objectives ( Babier et al., 2022 ) . A predictor first estimates the achievable three-dimensional (3D) dose distribution for a given anatomy, and a downstream optimization engine then determines the machine parameters whose delivered dose best matches it. The rationale behind dose mimicking is that the predicted dose encodes the clinical trade-offs from previously approved treatment plans, so that the optimizer focuses on achievable, patient-specific targets rather than on generic constraints that a clinician would need to specify and tune manually ( McIntosh et al., 2017 ) . Because the optimizer targets the predicted dose, errors in the prediction propagate into the delivered plan, making accurate prediction of the 3D dose distribution from the patient computed tomography (CT) scan, PTV volumes and OAR contours a critical intermediate step. Learning-based dose prediction was initially formulated as a deterministic regression task from the planning CT scan and the delineated PTV and OARs, solved by leveraging convolutional encoder-decoder-based architectures such as the 3D U-Net ( Liu et al., 2021 ) . Because a given anatomy admits a set of clinically valid plans that differ in how trade-offs were prioritized, the optimum of a regression trained against a single plan is the conditional mean over that set, which blurs the prediction and smooths the steep gradients separating target volumes from healthy tissue ( Feng et al., 2023 ) . To address this limitation, generative approaches were introduced, first with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) ( Zhan et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) , and more recently with diffusion models ( Feng et al., 2023 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) . The poor scalability of diffusion models in voxel space limited their use to two-dimensional (2D) slices in which consistency across slices is not modeled explicitly. Concurrently with the present work, Wang et al. (2026) demonstrated tractable volumetric diffusion by operating in a latent space obtained by transfer from a frozen video autoencoder pretrained on natural images. Diffusion in a latent space learned on dose distributions themselves, rather than transferred, has to our knowledge not been investigated. Whether deterministic or generative with fixed sampling, these methods return a single dose distribution for a given anatomy, and therefore commit to a specific set of choices in clinical trade-offs learned during training. In clinical practice, treatment planning requires balancing competing constraints with preferences and protocols varying across clinicians and institutions. The lack of efficient human-in-the-loop control has been identified as a challenge to the clinical integration of ATP ( Gao et al., 2025a ) . Two recent frameworks make these trade-offs adjustable. Gao et al. (2025a) introduce a preference penalty within a GAN-based framework, and Wang et al. (2026) align predictions to institutional preferences through reinforcement learning post-training. In both cases, the preference specification must be integrated into the training procedure in a supervised way, and Any2Any further assumes fixed planning preferences per institution, which is not verified clinically ( Nelms et al., 2012 ) . A second obstacle to the use of such models in clinics is how they are typically evaluated. Performance is almost always reported as the voxel-wise agreement with a single reference plan, together with dose-volume histogram (DVH)-derived error ( Babier et al., 2021 ) . These quantities measure the reproduction of one acceptable plan among the many possibilities rather than the clinical acceptability of the prediction. They are computed on grids, crops and normalizations that differ between studies, making inter-study direct comparisons difficult ( Kui et al., 2024 ; Zamanian et al., 2025 ) . Additionally, accuracy measured on the predicted dose does not guarantee the clinical acceptability of the plan generated from it. In their OpenKBP-Opt study, Babier et al. (2022) report a moderate positive correlation (Spearman, ρ \rho between 0.5 and 0.62) between dose prediction performance and plan quality; a model outperforming another one on dose prediction metrics will not always yield a better plan. Conventional dose prediction evaluation metrics are therefore necessary but insufficient evidence of the clinical acceptability of the plan that is ultimately delivered, which is rarely evaluated or reported. In this work, we use a cohort of 900 clinically delivered volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) plans coming from five centers in three countries, spanning a range of prescription levels, protocols and planning styles. The dataset retains the inter-institutional and inter-clinician variability which is removed by construction when using a dataset of plans generated by a single automated treatment planning solution as is the case in the public AAPM GDP-HMM cohort ( Gao et al., 2025b ) . Nonetheless, we also report results on this dataset to provide a benchmark against which future work can be compared directly. We introduce LaDose , a radiotherapy-specific latent diffusion framework for fully 3D dose prediction, trained on 900 clinically delivered plans from five centers in three countries. In a six-framework comparison on this cohort, LaDose is the only model without a statistically significant bias across dosimetric endpoints, and the first latent diffusion predictor evaluated in a blinded expert review. It systematically addresses three core challenges: the representation in which generation occurs, the injection and control of clinical intent, and the clinical validity of the resulting plans. Our contributions are as follows: 1. A dose-specific latent space for whole-volume generation. We learn a latent space that captures the manifold of physically and clinically plausible dose maps. Because a dose distribution is a smooth field constrained by the physics of delivery, this manifold admits aggressive compression—reaching a factor of 128, compared with 16 for the dose latent space of concurrent work ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Generation therefore proceeds on entire volumes on a single GPU, without spatial decomposition and without loss of global consistency. The framework overcomes the scalability limits of conventional diffusion approaches while embedding prior knowledge of valid dose distributions. This relieves the denoiser of the need to learn what a plausible dose distribution looks like, freeing its capacity for the conditioning-to-dose mapping. 2. A generation-aware latent geometry. Latent diffusion pipelines typically optimize the autoencoder solely for reconstruction, leaving the geometry of the latent space unconstrained away from the encoder outputs—precisely the region occupied by sampled latents. We instead adapt latent denoising regularization ( Yang et al., 2026 ) to dose distributions, exposing the autoencoder to the same denoising objective used by the downstream diffusion model. The resulting latent space keeps perturbed latents decodable to valid dose distributions, so that residual denoiser error manifests as small, physically plausible deviations in voxel space. This incurs a measurable cost in voxel-wise reconstruction fidelity (a quantity never queried at inference) and yields a substantial gain in the quality of the predicted doses. 3. Disentangled conditioning. We separate target geometry from prescription information. Prescribed dose levels are supplied as exact scalar values rather than being painted into the voxel grid, where resampling, interpolation, and latent compression would otherwise degrade them. 4. Multiscale classifier-free guidance. We introduce a guidance mechanism that modulates the influence of each conditioning signal at inference time. This enables prescription-level and planner-level control over the generated plan and accommodates inter-institutional planning diversity without per-institution retraining or additional supervised training. 5. Evaluation on deliverable plans. We integrate the predictor with a dose-mimicking direct aperture optimization engine and report deliverable plan quality against the corresponding clinical plans for 30 patients treated from 2020 onwards, ensuring the comparison reflects current clinical practice. Acceptability is further assessed in a blinded review by three senior radiation oncologists and one senior medical physicist across three countries. The remainder of this work is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on automated treatment planning, deep-learning-based dose prediction and generalization across institutions, especially in the head-and-neck (HN) region. Section 3 describes the proposed radiotherapy-specific latent representation, the associated 3D diffusion-based dose prediction model and its integration with a fully automated treatment planning pipeline. Section 4 details the dataset, implementation details, and the evaluation framework. Section 5 reports reconstruction and prediction performance, along with the clinical acceptability of the generated plans. Section 6 discusses the design choices, the scope of the clinical evaluation and the directions for future work.

sections.heading: 2.1 Automated Treatment Planning and Dose Mimicking
sections.text: Knowledge-based planning (KBP) refers to the use of previously accepted and delivered plans to estimate an achievable dose distribution given a new anatomy. Initial KBP methods relied on geometric descriptors of the patient anatomy and PTV distribution ( Wu et al., 2009 ) to infer organ-wise DVHs ( Appenzoller et al., 2012 ) . The latter were then used as objectives for treatment planning systems (TPS). This approach brought improvements in terms of plan consistency and quality, and was adopted commercially ( Hansen et al., 2016 ) . However, a DVH is a one-dimensional summary of a three-dimensional dose distribution which, by nature, does not encode spatial information; two identical DVHs can mask substantial differences in hot spot and gradient location. Because the prediction of the complete dose distribution removes this ambiguity, it has become the preferred formulation in current ATP pipelines ( Babier et al., 2022 ) . Indeed, it provides an achievable voxel-wise objective for machine parameter optimization without requiring a clinician to specify them ( McIntosh et al., 2017 ) .

sections.heading: 2.2 From Regression to Generative Dose Prediction
sections.text: Most existing frameworks formulate dose prediction as a deterministic voxel-wise regression task from CT; such approaches predominantly leverage U-Net-based architectures and their variants ( Kontaxis et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2021 ) , e.g., augmented with transformer components ( Hu et al., 2023 ) . Fully transformer-based architectures have been explored ( Wen et al., 2023 ) but are often limited to two-dimensional settings due to their high computational cost, a limitation that can be alleviated through latent-space compression of the input data ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Despite their success, regression-based methods are known to suffer from high-frequency detail loss ( Feng et al., 2023 ) and fail to integrate prior knowledge on the clinical and physical properties of valid dose distributions ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . This has led recent studies to formulate dose prediction as a generative modeling task. Approaches based on GANs ( Zhan et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) demonstrated improved local detail reconstruction, but are prone to unstable training and mode collapse ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . Diffusion models (DMs) have shown superior performance in recovering high frequency details, leading to their adoption in dose prediction pipelines ( Feng et al., 2023 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) . However, the computational cost of diffusion models in voxel space has confined most work to a slice-wise formulation. Concurrently with the present work, Wang et al. (2026) achieved fully volumetric diffusion-based dose prediction by operating in a latent space with a compression rate of 16. They leverage a frozen video autoencoder pretrained on natural images (Wan 2.1, 127 M parameters).

sections.heading: 2.3 Conditioning Signals
sections.text: The most common setting conditions on the planning CT, together with the PTV and OAR contours ( Liu et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2019 ; Gronberg et al., 2021 ) . Other models also supply geometric descriptors derived from the masks, in the form of signed distance maps, based on the hypothesis that the distance to the target boundary is a strong predictor of the dose distribution ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . A third family of approaches leverages the geometry of the delivered plan. Teng et al. (2024) generate binary beam masks to allow for downstream beam-wise decomposition and refinement of the predicted dose. The publicly available GDP-HMM dataset ( Gao et al., 2025b ) provides beam plates and an additional input modality, encoding delivery geometry ( Xiong et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Cao et al. (2025) combine beam trajectories with pencil-beam dose calculation to ground the prediction in the physics of the delivery. Reconstruction performance improves with this conditioning strength progression, along with the preprocessing burden. The handling of the prescription condition is largely inherited from the dataset on which each method is developed. The OpenKBP dataset ( Babier et al., 2021 ) contains a single prescription protocol (70/63/56 Gy). Associated released implementations commonly encode prescription by assigning the prescribed dose to the associated PTV contour ( Liu et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Uniform prescription protocols render the prescription condition uninformative and absorb it into the constant dose normalization ( Fu et al., 2024 ) . The GDP-HMM dataset ( Gao et al., 2025b ) contains multiple prescription protocols, and the prescription is encoded by assigning the prescribed dose to the associated PTV contour ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . When supplied, the prescribed dose is carried by a spatial input and undergoes the same resampling, interpolation and compression in the case of a latent formulation ( Wang et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 2.4 Clinical Preference Integration
sections.text: Two recent frameworks allow for the integration of clinical preferences. Gao et al. (2025a) introduce a homogeneity index and per OAR sliders, which can be manually tuned at inference time by the user to adjust OAR sparing or target coverage. To do so, they sample slider values during training and add a secondary supervised objective in the loss function of the model, which correlates slider values to dosimetric endpoints. Wang et al. (2026) align their dose prediction model to specific institutes via an additional reinforcement learning step, which requires retraining the model for each new institution.

sections.heading: 2.5 Generalization Across Institutions and Protocols
sections.text: Historically, dose prediction frameworks have been trained and evaluated on single-center cohorts of anatomical sites such as lung or prostate, or on intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) delivery. In an effort to enable generalization, the GDP-HMM challenge released a large dataset of IMRT and VMAT plans for multiple prescription protocols across the head-and-neck and thoracic regions ( Gao et al., 2025b ) . The plans are, however, generated automatically and thus follow a single, consistent planning style. The authors report that they have not been clinically approved at this stage. Due to the high density of critical anatomical structures and the use of VMAT as the predominant delivery mode ( Alfouzan, 2021 ) , accurate dose delivery is particularly challenging in the HN region ( Zamanian et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, heterogeneous evaluation practices and limited data availability further complicate progress in HN dose prediction ( Kui et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: VMAT Delivery and Treatment Planning
sections.text: External beam radiotherapy delivers ionizing radiation to the patient using a linear accelerator (LINAC). The LINAC gantry rotates around the patient, while the photon beam is shaped by a multi-leaf collimator (MLC) consisting of opposing rows of motorized tungsten leaves. The delivered radiation is quantified in monitor units (MU). In VMAT, gantry rotation, MLC leaf positions, and dose rate vary continuously and simultaneously ( Alfouzan, 2021 ) . For treatment planning, delivery is discretized into control points, each defining the gantry angle, dose rate, and MLC aperture. Inverse planning determines a sequence of control points whose accumulated dose achieves adequate target coverage while satisfying the clinical constraints imposed by neighboring OARs.

sections.heading: 3.2 Radiotherapy-Specific 3D Latent Representation
sections.text: Diffusion directly in voxel space is computationally prohibitive at the resolution of clinical dose distributions and therefore requires a compact latent representation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . The choice of latent space determines both the computational cost of diffusion and the complexity of the distribution that the denoising network must model. We therefore learn a radiotherapy-specific latent space directly from dose distributions rather than adopting a general-purpose latent representation designed for natural images. We use variational autoencoders (VAEs) to encode the different input modalities into compact volumetric representations. The diffusion process is performed entirely in the latent space, while a dedicated dose decoder maps generated dose latents back to voxel space. Because dose distributions are smooth scalar fields governed by the physics of radiation delivery, their intrinsic dimensionality is substantially lower than that of natural images. A dose-specific latent space can therefore exploit this structure to achieve high compression while retaining the spatial detail required for accurate dose prediction. In addition, the dose decoder implicitly captures the prior of plausible dose distributions, allowing the diffusion model to focus primarily on learning the conditional mapping from patient and treatment information to dose.

sections.heading: Generation-Aware Latent Space Regularization
sections.text: In latent diffusion models, the autoencoder is typically optimized independently of the downstream generative model. This creates a potential mismatch between training and inference: the decoder is trained primarily on z 0 z_{0} , the latent representations produced by the encoder, whereas during diffusion sampling it receives z ^ 0 \hat{z}_{0} , an estimate of the clean latent obtained after a finite number of denoising steps. Consequently, z ^ 0 \hat{z}_{0} may lie near, but not exactly on, the encoder’s latent manifold. If the decoder is poorly behaved in this neighborhood, small denoising errors can result in disproportionately large reconstruction errors in voxel space. We address this issue by explicitly shaping the latent space so that neighborhoods around encoded samples remain meaningful and smoothly decodable. Inspired by Yang et al. (2026) , training of the dose visual tokenizer is performed in two stages. In the first stage, encoder latents are interpolated with samples from a Gaussian prior before being passed to the decoder. For an encoded latent z z , we define z ′ = ( 1 − τ ) ​ z + τ ​ γ ​ ε , ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) , τ ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) , z^{\prime}=(1-\tau)z+\tau\gamma\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}),\qquad\tau\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1), (10) where γ \gamma controls the standard deviation of the Gaussian component and τ \tau determines the corruption level. The decoder is trained to reconstruct the original input from z ′ z^{\prime} . This latent corruption objective serves two complementary purposes. First, it regularizes the latent representation by discouraging information from being encoded in directions that are highly sensitive to small perturbations, resulting in a smoother latent geometry. Second, it aligns the autoencoder with the downstream diffusion task: the decoder is explicitly trained to map perturbed latent representations to valid dose distributions, rather than being optimized solely for reconstruction of encoder outputs. Consequently, deviations in latent space are more likely to produce gradual and physically plausible changes in the reconstructed dose. The first training stage exposes the decoder to the full range of corruption levels through the uniform sampling of τ \tau . However, inference primarily requires robustness to relatively small deviations around the clean latent, since the decoder receives the denoiser’s estimate z ^ 0 \hat{z}_{0} rather than an arbitrarily corrupted latent. Training exclusively on corrupted latents can therefore trade reconstruction fidelity for robustness in regions of latent space that are less relevant at inference. To recover high-fidelity reconstruction, we use a second training stage in which the encoder is frozen and the decoder is fine-tuned using clean latents only. The decoder is thus initialized from a solution that is robust to latent perturbations, while the second stage restores reconstruction fidelity on the encoder manifold.

sections.heading: Conditional 3D Latent Diffusion
sections.text: Dose prediction is formulated as conditional generation in the dose-specific latent space described in Section 3.2 . Let z 0 z_{0} denote the clean latent representation of the ground-truth dose distribution. The denoising network 𝒟 θ \mathcal{D}_{\theta} is trained to recover z 0 z_{0} from its noisy counterpart, conditioned on the latent representations of the planning CT, target structures, OARs, and prescription information. The denoising network 𝒟 θ \mathcal{D}_{\theta} is a three-dimensional U-Net with three resolution levels. Each level contains three residual blocks, with a self-attention layer at the bottleneck. The base channel width is 192, with channel multipliers of 1 1 , 2 2 , and 2 2 across the three resolutions. Training uses the ℒ 2 \mathcal{L}_{2} denoising objective together with the preconditioning scheme and log-normal noise distribution of Karras et al. (2022) . During inference, the generated dose latent is mapped to voxel space using the dose decoder. An overview of the complete framework is shown in Fig. 1 . Figure 1: Overview of the proposed 3D latent diffusion framework for dose prediction. Patient and treatment information are encoded into volumetric latent representations that condition a 3D diffusion model. The generated dose latent is subsequently decoded into a voxel-space dose distribution.

sections.heading: Disentangled Spatial and Prescription Conditioning
sections.text: We disentangle spatial and scalar conditioning to preserve prescription information while enabling spatial conditioning to propagate throughout the diffusion network. Jointly encoding a PTV volume with its associated prescription value would subject the scalar prescription information to spatial compression and may therefore degrade its numerical fidelity. Instead, spatial and scalar information are represented separately. Spatial conditioning is introduced by concatenating the latent embeddings of the PTV and other spatial structures with the noisy dose latent. Prescription information is represented independently as a vector p ∈ ℝ 3 p\in\mathbb{R}^{3} and transformed by a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) into a conditioning embedding e p e_{p} . Let e t e_{t} denote the timestep embedding. The two embeddings are combined as e = SiLU ⁡ ( e t + e p ) , e=\mathrm{SiLU}(e_{t}+e_{p}), (11) and projected into the feature space of each residual block. For an intermediate feature map h h , the resulting conditioning is injected additively as h ′ = h + W e ​ e , h^{\prime}=h+W_{e}e, (12) where W e W_{e} is a learned projection. Applying this modulation throughout the network ensures that prescription information is available at all depths while preserving its numerical representation independently of spatial compression.

sections.text: Dose prediction involves multiple conditioning signals with different clinical roles, and the desired balance between target coverage and OAR sparing may vary across patients and clinicians. To enable user-specific control over the predicted dose distribution, we implement multiscale classifier-free guidance ( Brooks et al., 2023 ) , which allows for the independent modulation of each conditioning modality at inference time. Let z σ z_{\sigma} denote a noisy dose latent at noise level σ \sigma , and let z ^ 0 𝒞 = 𝒟 θ ​ ( z σ , σ , 𝒞 ) \hat{z}_{0}^{\mathcal{C}}=\mathcal{D}_{\theta}(z_{\sigma},\sigma,\mathcal{C}) (13) denote the predicted clean dose latent under conditioning set 𝒞 \mathcal{C} . We define the conditioning hierarchy ∅ → CT → ( CT , PTV ) → ( CT , PTV , OAR ) , \varnothing\rightarrow\mathrm{CT}\rightarrow(\mathrm{CT},\mathrm{PTV})\rightarrow(\mathrm{CT},\mathrm{PTV},\mathrm{OAR}), (14) and compute the guided prediction as z ~ 0 \displaystyle\tilde{z}_{0} = z ^ 0 ∅ + s CT ​ ( z ^ 0 CT − z ^ 0 ∅ ) \displaystyle=\hat{z}_{0}^{\varnothing}+s_{\mathrm{CT}}\left(\hat{z}_{0}^{\mathrm{CT}}-\hat{z}_{0}^{\varnothing}\right) (15) + s PTV ​ ( z ^ 0 CT , PTV − z ^ 0 CT ) \displaystyle+s_{\mathrm{PTV}}\left(\hat{z}_{0}^{\mathrm{CT},\mathrm{PTV}}-\hat{z}_{0}^{\mathrm{CT}}\right) + s OAR ​ ( z ^ 0 CT , PTV , OAR − z ^ 0 CT , PTV ) , \displaystyle+s_{\mathrm{OAR}}\left(\hat{z}_{0}^{\mathrm{CT},\mathrm{PTV},\mathrm{OAR}}-\hat{z}_{0}^{\mathrm{CT},\mathrm{PTV}}\right), where s CT , s PTV , s OAR ≥ 0 s_{\mathrm{CT}},s_{\mathrm{PTV}},s_{\mathrm{OAR}}\geq 0 are independently adjustable guidance scales. Each scale controls the incremental contribution of the corresponding conditioning signal relative to the preceding level in the hierarchy. This formulation enables personalized dose generation without retraining the diffusion model or requiring additional labeled data.

sections.text: Figure 2: End-to-end automated treatment planning framework. Plans are generated with a commercially available, fully automated VMAT planning engine ( Prunaretty et al., 2024 ) , based on direct aperture optimization (DAO) (Fig. 2 ), which optimizes machine parameters directly rather than intermediate fluence maps. Let d ^ ∈ ℝ + N \hat{d}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{+} denote the generated dose resampled to the planning CT grid. Let x = ( ℓ , μ ) x=(\ell,\mu) be the concatenated MLC leaf positions ℓ \ell and the MU increments μ \mu of all control points of the arcs. With d ⁡ ( x ) d(x) denoting the dose delivered by x x , the machine parameters are obtained by solving the following optimization problem: min x ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ ∑ s ∈ 𝒪 w s | s | ​ ∑ i ∈ s [ d i ​ ( x ) − d ^ i ] + 2 ⏟ dose mimicking + ∑ s ∈ 𝒯 w s | s | ​ ∑ i ∈ s ( d i ​ ( x ) − p s ) 2 ⏟ target coverage + ℛ ⁡ ( x ) , \min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\;\underbrace{\sum_{s\in\mathcal{O}}\frac{w_{s}}{|s|}\sum_{i\in s}\Big[\,d_{i}(x)-\hat{d}_{i}\,\Big]_{+}^{2}}_{\text{dose mimicking}}\;+\;\underbrace{\sum_{s\in\mathcal{T}}\frac{w_{s}}{|s|}\sum_{i\in s}\big(d_{i}(x)-p_{s}\big)^{2}}_{\text{target coverage}}\;+\;\mathcal{R}(x), (16) where [ ⋅ ] + = max ⁡ ( ⋅ , 0 ) [\,\cdot\,]_{+}=\max(\cdot,0) , 𝒪 \mathcal{O} is the set of OAR contours and auxiliary structures such as overlaps, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} the set of targets, p s p_{s} the prescribed dose of target s s and w s w_{s} a structure weight. The predicted dose acts as voxel-wise upper bound on healthy tissue: the model is penalized when it exceeds the sparing that the dose prediction model considers achievable for this anatomy. Target volumes are optimized independently from the prediction to ensure that coverage is dependent on protocol rather than implicitly passed as a voxel-wise objective. For the left and right brachial plexuses, along with the spinal cord, an additional fixed clinical constraint is added as a one-sided quadratic penalty at fixed dose levels. To ensure the deliverability of the generated plans, the optimization is constrained to the set of machine-deliverable parameters 𝒳 \mathcal{X} and regularized by ℛ ⁡ ( x ) \mathcal{R}(x) . ℛ ⁡ ( x ) \mathcal{R}(x) comprises a penalty term on total MUs, a total-variation term smoothing the MU profile along each arc, and a leaf-edge term penalizing irregular aperture shapes. The set of machine-deliverable parameters 𝒳 \mathcal{X} is defined by the minimum and maximum MLC leaf gap, the leaf-carriage span, and the maximum leaf travel and MU per segment derived from the leaf-speed, gantry-speed and dose-rate limits of the treatment unit. The dose is calculated with a continuous aperture model that integrates the fluence delivered between consecutive control points rather than sampling static apertures at discrete gantry angles ( Christiansen et al., 2018 ) , from dose-influence matrices precomputed with a collapsed-cone convolution dose engine ( Ahnesjö, 1989 ) . The optimization problem is initialized with conformal apertures obtained from the beam’s-eye-view projection of the targets, refined by column generation ( Peng et al., 2012 ) and solved using first-order gradient descent. The final dose is recomputed with the same collapsed-cone dose engine at full resolution.

sections.heading: 4.1 Dataset
sections.text: This study is based on a multi-centric, retrospective dataset of 900 head-and-neck cancer patients treated with VMAT between 2018 and 2025, from five centers across three countries. Prescriptions ranged from 50 to 70 Gy across one to three levels of PTV. The cohort was split into training (n=753), validation (n=71), and test (n=76) sets. For each patient, data included planning CT, clinically delivered dose distribution, and tumor and OAR contours (brainstem, spinal cord, parotids, mandible). The distribution of primary tumor sites and of prescribed dose levels is reported in Table 1 . To our knowledge, this is the largest reported cohort of clinically approved VMAT plans used for dose prediction. Model performance was further assessed on the public AAPM GDP-HMM dataset ( Gao et al., 2025b ) restricted to the HN VMAT patients (472 training, 74 validation), with prescriptions from 50 to 70 Gy over one to three PTV levels. This cohort differs from ours in terms of planning protocol: plans were automatically generated by a single planning framework, and are correspondingly more homogeneous (median homogeneity index 4.27 4.27 against 7.67 7.67 percentage points on our in-house data). sections.heading: 4.2 Evaluation Metrics and Protocol
sections.text: All models assessed on our in-house dataset were trained at a single resolution and evaluated under a single protocol. No resampling was performed at inference time. Performance was assessed using the mean absolute error (MAE) and the DVH metric MAE from the OpenKBP challenge ( Babier et al., 2021 ) . As these metrics do not reflect the asymmetrical clinical impact of errors, we also report the Homogeneity Index (HI, HI = ( D 2 − D 98 ) / D 50 × 100 =(D_{2}-D_{98})/D_{50}\times 100 ), the Nakamura Conformity Index (nCI) ( Nakamura et al., 2001 ) and D 99 D_{99} , or dose received by 99% of the high-dose PTV to assess tumor coverage, as well as standard OAR DVH metrics to evaluate OAR sparing. The metrics were computed on the set of voxels restricted to the patient external contour, excluding the couch and immobilization devices. As the objective of the dose prediction step is to accurately reconstruct the clinical dose, we report the signed deviation of the predicted from the delivered dose of these additional metrics, rather than the absolute error. Evaluation on the AAPM GDP-HMM dataset was carried out using the same protocol, but in the geometry of the AAPM GDP-HMM dataset so that it is directly comparable with future work. The unit of analysis is the patient. Statistical significance was assessed using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, between each baseline and LaDose, as well as between each model and zero to assess systematic bias. p p -values are adjusted using the Holm–Bonferroni procedure.

sections.heading: 4.3 Baseline Models
sections.text: We compare against four published dose prediction models spanning the two dominant formulations: two convolutional regression networks, C3D ( Liu et al., 2021 ) and DCNN ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) , and two diffusion-based models, DoseDiff ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) and MD-Dose ( Fu et al., 2024 ) . Additionally, we include the winning entry of the AAPM 2025 GDP-HMM dose prediction challenge ( Abdulkadir and Neylon, 2025 ) , based on MedNeXt ( Roy et al., 2023 ) , as it defines the current state of the art on the largest public dose prediction dataset ( Gao et al., 2025b ) . We reproduce the single MedNeXt model rather than the challenge-winning ensemble of that model with the organizers’ baseline network. Each model was retrained from scratch on the training split of our cohort using the authors’ released implementation, and the best-performing checkpoint was selected for evaluation. Hyperparameters were kept as reported by the authors unless the original configuration was incompatible with our data or the model did not train properly. The adaptations fall into two main categories, and are reported in detail per model in Appendix A . First, the field of view and model resolution was adapted to match that of our dataset. Second, prescription conditioning was introduced in implementations that assumed a uniform protocol. Additional changes were made when the released code contained defects that prevented training or inference: for instance, the released MD-Dose implementation sampled the latent prior using min-max normalization, which introduced a mismatch with the noise injected during training and resulted in a high MAE on our test set. Any correction improved the baseline, and we report the best achieved results throughout. On the AAPM GDP-HMM dataset, we compare against the winner’s released checkpoint on the challenge’s own data, including the beam geometry conditioning ( Gao et al., 2025b ; Abdulkadir and Neylon, 2025 ) . The two models operate under different conditioning regimes which favor the challenge model.

sections.heading: Data Processing
sections.text: Volumes were resampled to an in-plane resolution of 1.27 × 1.27 1.27\times 1.27 mm, with a slice spacing of 2.5 2.5 mm. Each volume was cropped to a fixed size of 256 × 256 × 192 256\times 256\times 192 using the center of the bounding box of the high-dose PTV as the volume center. Voxels outside the patient external contour, including couch components and immobilization devices, were removed using masking. Dose and prescription values were linearly rescaled from [ 0 , 80 ] [0,80] Gy to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] ; CT intensities were clipped to [ − 1024 , 1900 ] [-1024,1900] HU and linearly rescaled to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] .

sections.heading: Dose Variational Autoencoder
sections.text: VAEs use downsampling factors 8 × 8 × 4 8\times 8\times 4 and were trained patch-wise using Adam (lr 10 − 4 10^{-4} , linear warm-up, β = 1.0 \beta=1.0 , batch size 8) on 4 RTX 3090 GPUs. Following the training process described in Section 3.2 , we train the dose VAE with latent corruption for 2800 epochs, then freeze the encoder and further fine-tune the decoder for 560 epochs. The interpolation noise scale is set to γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 to match the learned latent distribution.

sections.heading: 3D Diffusion Model
sections.text: The diffusion model was trained on full volumes for 140,000 steps on a single RTX 3090 with Adam (lr 10 − 4 10^{-4} , linear warm-up, batch size 8) and the noise schedule of Karras et al. (2022) . Inference leverages a deterministic ODE, Heun-EDM sampling and 20 denoising steps. Predictions were clamped to [ 0 , 1.06 × prescription ] [0,1.06\times\text{prescription}] .

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.text: We perform an incremental ablation study to assess the contribution of each component. To the baseline, we gradually introduce conditioning disentanglement (DisCond), latent denoising regularization (DenoReg) and multiscale classifier-free guidance (mCFG). Each variant was trained with the same schedule, budget and random seed. Evaluation was conducted under the same protocol as described in Section 4.2 , on the test set. By construction, classifier-free guidance operates only at inference; the corresponding ablation compares sampling with per-modality scales against sampling with a single scale applied to the combined conditioning set.

sections.heading: Evaluation on the AAPM GDP-HMM Dataset
sections.text: For this experiment, we keep our autoencoder unchanged and retrain only the denoising network under the same budget and hyperparameter configuration. The latent space thus remains the one learned on our in-house dataset. The challenge’s model is evaluated as released. Our model operates at a different resolution; we resample our predictions onto the challenge’s grid, placing the cost of the interpolation on our model.

sections.heading: Inference-Time Controllability Study
sections.text: Inference-time controllability is characterized by multiple linear regression analysis between guidance scales and normalized dose quality metrics. We sampled a subset of 20 patients from the test set cohort at random, and generated 144 predictions per patient with guidance scales ( s CT , s PTV , s OAR ) (s_{\mathrm{CT}},s_{\mathrm{PTV}},s_{\mathrm{OAR}}) drawn from a grid spanning [ 1.0 , 2.2 ] [1.0,2.2] for the CT scale and [ 1.0 , 4.0 ] [1.0,4.0] for the PTV and OAR scales. All other hyperparameters were fixed. DVH metrics were standardized with zero mean and unit variance before being regressed against each individual scale to allow for direct magnitude comparison. Monotonicity of the response was assessed by varying one scale at a time over its specific range, aggregating and averaging the resulting DVH metrics across the different scale combinations.

sections.heading: 4.5.1 Direct Aperture Optimization Implementation Details
sections.text: All plans were generated with two coplanar full arcs ( − 179 ∘ → 179 ∘ -179^{\circ}\rightarrow 179^{\circ} clockwise and back counter-clockwise) with static collimator angles of − 30 ∘ -30^{\circ} and + 30 ∘ +30^{\circ} , a control point every 2 ∘ 2^{\circ} (179 per arc), dose-influence matrices computed every 8 ∘ 8^{\circ} on a 5 5 mm bixel grid, and a single isocenter placed at the centroid of the target volumes. Plans were computed for three different LINAC models: an Elekta Versa HD with a flattened 6 MV beam, a Varian Halcyon with a 6 MV flattening-filter-free beam, and a Varian TrueBeam with a high-definition MLC and a flattened 6 MV beam. Each patient was planned using the configuration of the machine that delivered the treatment, so that each automated plan and its associated clinical plan could be compared directly. Additionally, the clinically approved, delivered plans were recalculated using the same collapsed-cone dose engine.

sections.heading: 4.5.2 Blinded Clinical Review and Quantitative Comparison
sections.text: As a proof of concept, the complete automated planning framework was assessed in a blinded reader study. Thirty patients were drawn at random from the test set, restricted to those treated from 2020 onwards to ground the study in contemporary clinical practice. Each patient contributed a single plan, either the delivered clinical plan or the automated plan, assigned at random (15 per arm); plans were never presented side by side, so that reviewers could not determine provenance by comparison. Four reviewers from three countries – three senior radiation oncologists and one senior medical physicist – each assessed a random subset of 20 of the 30 plans, blinded to plan provenance and to one another’s assessments. Reviewers were shown the calculated plans along with DVH metrics and compliance with clinical constraints, using a conventional treatment planning system interface developed in-house. They rated each plan as acceptable as is, acceptable after minor editing, or not acceptable. Independently of the reader study, the 30 plan pairs were analyzed quantitatively. For each patient, the automated plan and the delivered clinical plan were compared on the basis of standard DVH metrics, computed from the exported DICOM RT Plan objects after dose recalculation using a collapsed-cone-based dose engine. Total MU were compared as a surrogate for plan complexity and delivery efficiency. Statistical significance was tested with two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

sections.heading: 5 Results
sections.text: We evaluate LaDose in three stages. First, we quantify the reconstruction fidelity of the dose variational autoencoder, including the effect of latent denoising regularization and its transfer to the AAPM GDP-HMM external cohort. We then assess the generative model’s dose prediction accuracy on the in-house test set and the external cohort, together with ablation, generalization, and controllability analyses. Finally, we examine the clinical relevance of our approach by assessing the quality and acceptability of the plans generated by our end-to-end planning pipeline integrated with LaDose as a predictor.

sections.heading: Reconstruction Capacity
sections.text: Because the decoder bounds the performance of any denoiser on its latent space, we first characterize the learned representation. Table 2 reports the agreement between the delivered dose and its reconstruction through the encoder and decoder of Section 3.2 under the evaluation protocol described in Section 4.2 . At a compression rate of 128, the autoencoder reproduces the delivered dose with a median MAE of 0.135 Gy and a median DVH score of 0.160 Gy, well below the prediction error of the best-performing denoiser (Table 3 ). This confirms that the representation does not limit the downstream predictive accuracy on our in-house dataset.

sections.heading: Impact of Latent Denoising Regularization
sections.text: Latent denoising regularization trades voxel-wise reconstruction fidelity for decodability of perturbed latents. We examine its impact on the reconstruction quality before examining its effect on generation. Indeed, training the decoder on strongly corrupted latents degraded voxel-wise reconstruction from 0.135 Gy to 0.217 Gy, while fine-tuning on clean samples recovered part of this loss, yielding a median MAE of 0.160 0.160 Gy ( p = 2.5 × 10 − 14 p=2.5\times 10^{-14} ). The complete procedure remains worse voxel-wise than the baseline, but significantly improves reconstruction in PTVs and OARs, as illustrated by the removal of the systematic under-coverage of the high-dose PTV (from − 0.139 -0.139 Gy to + 0.039 +0.039 Gy in D 99 D_{99} , p = 0.02 p=0.02 ; no detectable bias for the complete protocol only). The improvement is also reflected in the conformity index, which remains biased but falls by a factor of 5 (from − 0.0139 -0.0139 to + 0.0026 +0.0026 , p = 0.02 p=0.02 ). These improvements, which are more significant clinically than voxel-wise reconstruction, are consistent with the design rationale described in Section 3.2 . The gain is made even clearer when looking at generative performance (see Section 5.2 ), as the denoising pre-training component is the largest contributor to prediction quality. The trade of voxel-wise reconstruction fidelity for a more structured and learnable latent distribution is consistent with what Yang et al. (2026) report for natural images. sections.heading: Overall Accuracy on the In-House Test Set
sections.text: Table 3 summarizes the performance of LaDose against the five baselines on the held-out test set; Fig. 5 illustrates examples of dose distributions predicted by LaDose. Our model achieved the lowest voxel-wise error among published baselines, with a median MAE of 1.18 1.18 Gy ( p ≤ 1.3 × 10 − 8 p\leq 1.3\times 10^{-8} ); the retrained GDP-HMM challenge winner, MedNeXt, matched it at 1.16 1.16 Gy, a difference that is not significant ( p = 1.00 p=1.00 ). On the DVH score, LaDose performed significantly better than C3D, DCNN, MD-Dose ( p ≤ 1.6 × 10 − 8 p\leq 1.6\times 10^{-8} ) and MedNeXt ( p = 1.6 × 10 − 3 p=1.6\times 10^{-3} ), while being statistically indistinguishable from DoseDiff. No baseline was competitive on both metrics simultaneously: MedNeXt matched LaDose on MAE but not on the DVH score, and DoseDiff the opposite. In addition to the OpenKBP aggregate metrics, we further assess performance using the conventional radiotherapy metrics described in Section 4.2 . DCNN systematically under-covered the high-dose target by a median of 2.43 2.43 Gy, an offset that the MAE column did not uncover. C3D, DCNN, DoseDiff and MedNeXt all predicted more conformal doses than were delivered ( Δ \Delta nCI − 0.090 -0.090 , − 0.109 -0.109 , − 0.040 -0.040 , − 0.059 -0.059 respectively), while MD-Dose predicted a less conformal one ( Δ \Delta nCI 0.025 0.025 ); all these deviations are significant. With regard to OAR sparing, both diffusion baselines systematically over-dosed the brainstem and spinal cord: DoseDiff by 2.11 2.11 Gy and 1.97 1.97 Gy, and MD-Dose by 2.63 2.63 Gy and 1.70 1.70 Gy. In contrast, C3D systematically under-dosed the spinal cord and parotids by − 2.13 -2.13 Gy and − 0.67 -0.67 Gy respectively. Because it can set an unachievable target, under-prediction can be a cause of optimization failure in a dose-mimicking pipeline. LaDose was the only model whose predictions did not differ significantly from the delivered plans across the seven metrics. By contrast, C3D and MedNeXt were biased on three, DCNN on four, DoseDiff on six and MD-Dose on five. sections.heading: Evaluation on the AAPM GDP-HMM Cohort
sections.text: By retraining our denoiser on the AAPM GDP-HMM cohort, we aim to place the model on a public benchmark rather than assert superiority over the challenge winner. Indeed, our model is deliberately not conditioned on delivery parameters (see Section 6 ) which does not enable relevant direct comparison. The behavior observed on our in-house dataset is reproduced (Table 4 ); the challenge winner is more accurate voxel-wise (median MAE 1.23 1.23 against 1.57 1.57 Gy), while LaDose is more accurate on dosimetric endpoints (median DVH score 0.88 0.88 against 1.03 1.03 Gy). The difference is concentrated in tissue that carries no dosimetric constraint, in which the dose distribution is highly dependent on the geometry of the delivery. LaDose predicts a target dose 1.13 1.13 percentage points less homogeneous than the reference dose and under-covers the high-dose target by 0.80 0.80 Gy, while the challenge model is biased in the opposite direction, and significantly on brainstem near-maximum dose. Part of our model’s deviation can be explained by the decoder’s reconstruction bias: decoding the delivered dose through the autoencoder shifts D 99 D_{99} by − 0.38 -0.38 Gy and HI by + 0.22 +0.22 percentage points, which is consistent with the observed bias in the predicted dose and the difference in planning style between the two cohorts. sections.heading: Ablation of Model Components
sections.text: Table 5 reports the contribution of each component, evaluated under the protocol described in Section 4.2 . Disentangled conditioning lowered the median MAE from 1.34 1.34 to 1.28 1.28 Gy and improved 51 51 of the 76 76 test patients ( p = 0.010 p=0.010 before correction), but the difference did not survive correction ( p Holm = 0.09 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.09 ). Its contribution is therefore consistent in direction on voxel-wise accuracy, and we maintain the component on the design grounds given in Section 3 . Latent denoising regularization significantly improved prediction performance, lowering the median MAE to 1.18 1.18 Gy ( p Holm = 5.2 × 10 − 10 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=5.2\times 10^{-10} ) and the DVH score from 1.34 1.34 to 1.19 1.19 Gy ( p Holm = 1.6 × 10 − 5 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=1.6\times 10^{-5} ). Regarding dosimetric endpoints, target homogeneity and parotid mean dose improved ( p Holm = 0.049 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.049 and 0.042 0.042 ). Both configurations trained without it predicted a target dose consistently less homogeneous than delivered ( Δ \Delta HI + 1.05 +1.05 and + 0.88 +0.88 percentage points, p Holm < 10 − 3 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<10^{-3} ), the only endpoint on which either was biased; with it the deviation falls to − 0.09 -0.09 percentage points ( p Holm = 1.00 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=1.00 ), with no significant bias. Denoising pre-training acts on the quality of the dose representation rather than on the denoising network. The result supports the claim of the present work: the fidelity of the prediction is highly dependent on the learned latent space. Because multiscale guidance acts only at inference, the last two rows sample the checkpoint of the preceding row with per-modality scales rather than a single scale. The effect sizes quoted below are medians, across the test patients, of the within-patient difference between the two configurations, which is the paired quantity the Wilcoxon test is computed on; they therefore do not in general equal the difference between the corresponding cells of Table 5 , each of which is a cohort median taken independently. Raising s PTV s_{\mathrm{PTV}} from 1.4 1.4 to 1.8 1.8 increased target coverage ( D 99 D_{99} + 0.31 +0.31 Gy, p Holm = 3.5 × 10 − 12 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=3.5\times 10^{-12} ), improved homogeneity (HI − 0.24 -0.24 pp) and conformity (nCI − 0.011 -0.011 ), while raising parotid D mean D_{\mathrm{mean}} by 0.15 0.15 Gy; MAE, DVH score, brainstem and spinal cord maximum doses were left unchanged ( p Holm = 1.00 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=1.00 ). In contrast, raising s OAR s_{\mathrm{OAR}} to 4.0 4.0 reversed the trade: all four OAR dosimetric endpoints fell significantly (spinal cord D 0.1 ​ cc D_{0.1\mathrm{cc}} − 0.82 -0.82 Gy, mandible − 0.59 -0.59 Gy, brainstem − 0.63 -0.63 Gy, parotids − 0.48 -0.48 Gy, all p Holm < 10 − 8 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<10^{-8} ), concurrently and significantly lowering target coverage ( D 99 D_{99} − 0.53 -0.53 Gy). sections.heading: Generalization Across Tumor Sites and Prescriptions
sections.text: Most published dose prediction models are developed on cohorts limited to a single tumor site and prescription protocol (see Section 2 ), while LaDose is designed to generalize across the head-and-neck region. In addition to aggregate metrics which could mask subgroup-specific failures, we stratify the test cohort by primary tumor site and nominal prescription dose and report associated evaluation metrics. Results are reported in Fig. 6 . The model’s performance was consistent across the five primary tumor sites (Kruskal–Wallis p ≥ 0.36 p\geq 0.36 ), and every subgroup median lay within 0.4 0.4 Gy of the whole-cohort median on both error metrics. Target coverage remained unbiased, with the largest deviation being − 0.47 -0.47 Gy in the hypopharynx group ( n = 11 n=11 , 95% CI − 1.11 -1.11 to + 1.42 +1.42 ). Across prescription groups, the DVH metrics behaved similarly, while the voxel-wise error increased with the primary target prescription value from a median MAE of 0.78 0.78 Gy at 54 54 – 57.5 57.5 Gy to 1.28 1.28 Gy at 69 69 – 70 70 Gy ( p = 0.009 p=0.009 ). When expressed as a fraction of the prescription, the error is 1.4 1.4 – 1.8 % 1.8\% in every group and the difference is no longer detectable ( p = 0.16 p=0.16 ), indicating that the increase in absolute error is a reflection of the scale of the quantity being predicted rather than a loss of accuracy. The remaining metrics, reported in Tables 9 and 10 , showed no heterogeneity either ( p ≥ 0.075 p\geq 0.075 ); only D 99 D_{99} is plotted, being the only metric whose subgroup intervals are small enough to be informative ( 95 % 95\% half-width 0.5 0.5 – 1.5 1.5 Gy in the four named sites, against up to 7 7 Gy for the OAR endpoints). With 6 6 to 45 45 patients per stratum and site and prescription level inherently dependent, the analysis is descriptive. The results support the claim that no tumor site and no prescription protocol behaves as a systematic failure mode of the model. sections.heading: Inference-Time Controllability via Multiscale Guidance
sections.text: Control over the predicted dose at inference is what enables a single trained model to adapt to the planning preferences of users from different institutions (see Section 2 ). We therefore characterize inference-time controllability using multiple linear regression analysis between guidance scales and normalized dose quality metrics. Significance is reported after Holm correction across the metric–scale pairs. The PTV scale exhibited the strongest influence on the prediction, sharpening the gradient at the tumor boundary (nCI: β = − 0.72 \beta=-0.72 , 95% confidence interval [ − 0.82 , − 0.62 ] [-0.82,-0.62] , p Holm < 0.001 p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001 ), with the cohort mean nCI decreasing monotonically from 1.33 1.33 to 1.27 1.27 across s PTV ∈ [ 1 , 4 ] s_{\mathrm{PTV}}\in[1,4] . As expected, the same scale acted in the opposite direction on normal tissue, increasing parotid D mean D_{\mathrm{mean}} ( β = 0.87 \beta=0.87 , [ 0.84 , 0.90 ] [0.84,0.90] ), brainstem D max D_{\mathrm{max}} ( β = 0.83 \beta=0.83 , [ 0.81 , 0.85 ] [0.81,0.85] ) and spinal cord D max D_{\mathrm{max}} ( β = 0.70 \beta=0.70 , [ 0.67 , 0.73 ] [0.67,0.73] ). The OAR scale acted in the opposite direction on all three (spinal cord D max D_{\mathrm{max}} : β = − 0.76 \beta=-0.76 , [ − 0.79 , − 0.74 ] [-0.79,-0.74] ; brainstem D max D_{\mathrm{max}} : β = − 0.64 \beta=-0.64 , [ − 0.66 , − 0.62 ] [-0.66,-0.62] ; parotid D mean D_{\mathrm{mean}} : β = − 0.51 \beta=-0.51 , [ − 0.55 , − 0.48 ] [-0.55,-0.48] ), at the cost of target coverage (PTV high {}_{\text{high}} D 99 D_{99} : β = − 0.63 \beta=-0.63 , [ − 0.71 , − 0.54 ] [-0.71,-0.54] ). The CT scale was the only one whose effect on OAR dose was negligible ( | β | ≤ 0.10 |\beta|\leq 0.10 for all three organs); it acted instead on agreement with the clinical plan (dose score: β = − 0.69 \beta=-0.69 , [ − 0.74 , − 0.63 ] [-0.74,-0.63] ). The PTV and OAR channels therefore act as opposing controls on the trade-off between tumor coverage and OAR sparing, while the anatomical channel is the only one that does not displace dose between them. The linear model explained most of the variation in the dose quality metrics, with R 2 = 0.91 R^{2}=0.91 for the dose score, 0.66 0.66 for the conformity index, and 0.99 0.99 , 0.98 0.98 and 0.97 0.97 for brainstem D max D_{\mathrm{max}} , spinal cord D max D_{\mathrm{max}} and parotid D mean D_{\mathrm{mean}} respectively. Homogeneity is the one metric whose response is not monotonic: it improves up to s PTV ≈ 1.8 s_{\mathrm{PTV}}\approx 1.8 and degrades beyond it, with cohort mean values spanning 7.87 7.87 – 8.52 8.52 percentage points; we report HI as a response curve only. Fig. 7 shows the corresponding response curves, which illustrate how CFG enables the predictable modulation of clinical trade-offs at inference. sections.heading: Quantitative Comparison with Clinical Plans
sections.text: A predicted dose is not a treatment plan; it is used as a voxel-wise objective that an optimizer converts into a deliverable set of machine parameters (see Section 3.4 ). The quality of the plan depends on both the predictor and the optimizer’s performances ( Babier et al., 2022 ) . We therefore investigate clinical applicability of LaDose by integrating it into an end-to-end automated treatment planning pipeline and evaluating the resulting 30 plans against their delivered counterparts. Our ATP pipeline produced the 30 plans from planning CT, prescription and contours with a median planning time of 15.2 min. Automated plans were significantly less modulated than their delivered counterparts, with a median within-patient reduction of 67 MU per fraction ( − 9.6 % -9.6\% of the clinical median of 693 MU; mean 617 versus 729 MU) and a standard deviation of 77 versus 198 MU, consistent with the fixed two-arc geometry. The framework achieved superior OAR sparing (Table 6 ), with median reductions of 4.1 Gy to the right parotid, 2.4 Gy to the left parotid, 2.4 Gy to the mandible, and 3.8 Gy to the spinal cord and 1.6 Gy to the brainstem in near-maximum dose. The overall maximum dose received by the patient was reduced by 2.2 Gy. Target coverage was maintained, with high-dose PTV D 95 D_{95} only 0.57 Gy lower in the automated plans (95% CI − 0.85 -0.85 to − 0.40 -0.40 Gy) and all plans satisfying the clinical constraint of D 95 > 95 % D_{95}>95\% of the prescription. The automated plans were generated using the available contours. Inter-institutional protocol discrepancies result in heterogeneous contouring practices. The results summarized in Table 6 consider only the structures contoured in every patient. The results for structures which were not systematically contoured can be found in the appendix (Table 8 ). sections.heading: Blinded Expert Acceptability Study
sections.text: Automatic plans were systematically rated as clinically acceptable, with 14 out of 15 requiring no editing (against 1 out of 15 for the delivered plans—the majority did not reach consensus; Table 7 ). In contrast, four clinical plans were found to require re-planning by at least one reviewer, against none for the automated plans. Automated planning favored consensus among clinicians, with experts agreeing with one another on 13 of the 14 automated plans carrying two independent ratings or more, against 2 out of 14 clinical plans ( p = 6.9 × 10 − 5 p=6.9\times 10^{-5} ; Table 7 ). This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that our end-to-end planning pipeline is able to produce plans that are clinically acceptable without editing according to state-of-the-art clinical practice. Further clinical evaluation is out of this project’s scope, but is a promising future direction. sections.heading: Radiotherapy-Specific Latent Representation
sections.text: In their concurrent work, Wang et al. (2026) also perform volumetric latent diffusion, but obtain their representation by transfer from an autoencoder pretrained on natural videos. The latter is kept frozen, while the diffusion transformer is adapted to the dose prediction task. The present work takes a different path and learns the representation on dose distributions directly. Two consequences follow. Our framework leverages a smaller denoising network (1.3 B for the Wan 2.1 diffusion transformer, against 67 M for ours), which makes training and design iterations more tractable. Because the representation is not required to encode the high fidelity details of natural scenes, it allows for a substantially higher compression rate (128 versus 16 for Any2Any).

sections.heading: Conditioning Signal Design Choices
sections.text: Models supplied with beam configuration conditioning consistently improve on reconstruction metrics ( Teng et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2025 ; Xiong et al., 2026 ) . We deliberately omit this signal from our framework as the delivery geometry is an output of the treatment planning procedure rather than an input naturally available at prediction time. Nonetheless, the present work is compatible with beam-conditioned models, and the proposed framework could be extended to include beam geometry in the future.

sections.heading: Clinical Relevance of the Fully Automated Planning Pipeline
sections.text: We do not claim that the quality of the plans produced by the end-to-end pipeline is directly linked to the performance of our dose prediction model. We consider the complete pipeline as a unit, and claim that its different components work together to produce plans deemed clinically acceptable by senior clinicians. The moderate correlation between dose prediction metrics and plan quality reported by Babier et al. (2022) is why we report both rather than treat plan quality as a corollary of predictive accuracy.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: Several limitations of the present work should be acknowledged. In our current implementation, guidance scales are an abstract quantity which may be difficult for clinicians to interpret. A slider which maps this scale to a concrete DVH objective, together with per-organ rather than a pooled OAR scale, is a promising direction for future work. We decide to remove the variability inherent to sampling with a diffusion model during inference to ensure reproducibility at the cost of diversity. Studying this stochasticity and its potential benefits for uncertainty-aware planning is a natural extension. Finally, the end-to-end pipeline was compared against clinical plans but not against plans generated by the same optimizer integrated with a different predictor, so the contribution of prediction fidelity to overall plan quality cannot be formally isolated.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we presented and evaluated LaDose, a fully volumetric, prescription-conditioned, controllable, latent-diffusion-based dose prediction model for head-and-neck VMAT radiotherapy. We demonstrated that learning a structured dose latent representation enabled tractable 3D diffusion on a single GPU, and that aligning the decoder with the denoising task rather than treating it as a preprocessing step significantly contributed to predictive accuracy (Table 5 ). Our multiscale guidance mechanism allowed for predictable modulation of the trade-off between target coverage and OAR sparing at inference, which addresses inter-clinician variability without requiring preferences to be specified before training (Fig. 7 ). LaDose reached a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy (1.4–1.8% of the prescription), and was the only model of six without a statistically significant bias in any evaluated dosimetric endpoint. The plans produced by our end-to-end treatment planning pipeline with a median time of 15.2 minutes were rated clinically acceptable without editing in 14 of 15 cases (Table 7 ) in a blinded review by three senior radiation oncologists and one medical physicist across three countries.

sections.heading: Appendix A Reimplementation of Baseline Methods
sections.text: Baselines were retrained from scratch on our in-house dataset with the authors’ released implementation, and evaluated under the protocol of Section 4.2 . Three main adaptations were implemented: the field of view and voxel grid were set to the 256 × 256 × 192 256\times 256\times 192 crop at 1.27 × 1.27 × 2.5 1.27\times 1.27\times 2.5 mm used throughout this work; prescription conditioning was introduced wherever the released implementation assumed a uniform prescription protocol. The structure channels were remapped to the five contours available in our cohort. Every method is scored against the same reference dose and the same structures. In each case, the checkpoint minimizing the validation dose score was retained. DCNN required no further adaptation, while other model-specific changes are detailed below.

sections.heading: C3D
sections.text: is the two-stage cascade of 3D U-Nets that won the OpenKBP challenge ( Liu et al., 2021 ; Babier et al., 2021 ) . In order to train the model on our higher resolution grid, we trained C3D patch-wise, with a crop containing the PTVs (as in our model). Inference uses a sliding window with Gaussian weighting.

sections.heading: DoseDiff
sections.text: is a slice-wise conditional DDPM ( T = 1000 T=1000 , DDIM sampling with S = 8 S=8 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ). We normalize the dose and PTV channels by 80 Gy rather than the 75 Gy in the paper, as the maximum delivered dose in our cohort is 77.4 Gy. We match and follow three elements of the released training schedule that the paper does not describe: a 1000-step learning-rate warm-up, gradient clipping, and a single × 0.1 \times 0.1 learning-rate decay.

sections.heading: MD-Dose
sections.text: is a slice-wise conditional DDPM ( T = 1000 T=1000 ) whose Mamba-UNet denoiser is conditioned on a five-channel structure image (CT, three PTV masks, OAR label map) ( Fu et al., 2024 ) . Four adaptations were made, in order to address a discrepancy between the released code and the paper’s description or change a setting under which the model did not train. First, we normalized the dose and PTV channels by a fixed 80 Gy rather than the released per-patient min–max, which is not suitable to a multi-prescription setting. Second, the released implementation samples the initial latent from a min–max rescaled latent of mean 0.5 0.5 and standard deviation 0.1 0.1 , whereas training injects ε ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 ) \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) ; we matched inference to training sampling, which significantly improved the validation MAE. Third, the reported initial learning rate of 10 − 2 10^{-2} diverged on our data, so we adopted the 10 − 4 10^{-4} of the released code. Fourth, our training split yields over 7000 7000 optimizer steps per epoch against roughly 1250 1250 for the authors’ cohort; we match their training budget in steps rather than epochs to make retraining tractable.

sections.heading: MedNeXt
sections.text: is the winning entry of the AAPM 2025 GDP-HMM challenge ( Abdulkadir and Neylon, 2025 ) . The challenge introduces two additional delivery geometry input channels, which were zeroed out in our reimplementation. We note that the system that won the challenge is a voxel-wise equal-weight ensemble of this model with the organizers’ baseline network; we reproduce the single MedNeXt model only.

Komodakis Abstract Automated treatment planning (ATP) aims to reduce the unwarranted inter-planner variability of manual planning, while improving treatment quality and efficiency. Most ATP pipelines rely on the prediction of the achievable three-dimensional dose distribution for a given anatomy and the subsequent optimization of machine parameters to reproduce it. Diffusion-based methods are largely slice-wise due to the high dimensionality of radiotherapy data, and assume a one-to-one mapping between anatomy and optimal dose despite the multi-objective nature of treatment planning. They are evaluated on their ability to match reference doses and rarely on their integration in ATP frameworks. We present LaDose, a latent diffusion framework for fully volumetric dose prediction. An autoencoder learned on dose distributions, trained so that perturbed latents decode to plausible doses, compresses dose maps 128-fold and enables 3D diffusion on a single GPU. Prescription values are represented as exact scalar vectors that bypass the image encoder, avoiding resampling and latent compression. Multiscale classifier-free guidance allows for the modulation of clinical trade-offs at inference, without retraining or additional labeled data. On 900 clinically delivered head-and-neck volumetric modulated arc therapy plans from five centers, LaDose reached a median absolute error of 1.18 Gy (1.4–1.8% of the prescription) and was the only one of six frameworks free of systematic bias with respect to the reference distribution. Guidance scales acted predictably on target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing.
