Treatment planning is a highly complex and time-consuming inverse optimization process, aiming to deliver a prescribed dose to the planning target volume (PTV), while sparing surrounding organs at risk (OARs). Traditionally, dosimetrists manually adjust beam parameters and structure-specific objectives to iteratively refine the plan until it satisfies protocol constraints. As the trade-offs achievable for a given anatomy are not known a priori, this process is a manual search whose stopping point is determined by the time available and by the planner’s experience ( Hussein et al., 2018 ) . As a consequence, manual planning introduces wide inter-planner variability, including in the compliance with the constraints that determine clinical acceptability ( Nelms et al., 2012 ) . Part of this variability reflects different institutional protocols and clinician preferences, which an automated replacement must take into account explicitly. The remainder stems from limited planning time and expertise, and is the variability that automated treatment planning (ATP) aims to remove through standardization, improving plan quality and consistency while reducing planning time ( Momin et al., 2021 ) . Modern ATP pipelines often rely on direct aperture optimization with dose-mimicking objectives ( Babier et al., 2022 ) . A predictor first estimates the achievable three-dimensional (3D) dose distribution for a given anatomy, and a downstream optimization engine then determines the machine parameters whose delivered dose best matches it. The rationale behind dose mimicking is that the predicted dose encodes the clinical trade-offs from previously approved treatment plans, so that the optimizer focuses on achievable, patient-specific targets rather than on generic constraints that a clinician would need to specify and tune manually ( McIntosh et al., 2017 ) . Because the optimizer targets the predicted dose, errors in the prediction propagate into the delivered plan, making accurate prediction of the 3D dose distribution from the patient computed tomography (CT) scan, PTV volumes and OAR contours a critical intermediate step. Learning-based dose prediction was initially formulated as a deterministic regression task from the planning CT scan and the delineated PTV and OARs, solved by leveraging convolutional encoder-decoder-based architectures such as the 3D U-Net ( Liu et al., 2021 ) . Because a given anatomy admits a set of clinically valid plans that differ in how trade-offs were prioritized, the optimum of a regression trained against a single plan is the conditional mean over that set, which blurs the prediction and smooths the steep gradients separating target volumes from healthy tissue ( Feng et al., 2023 ) . To address this limitation, generative approaches were introduced, first with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) ( Zhan et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) , and more recently with diffusion models ( Feng et al., 2023 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) . The poor scalability of diffusion models in voxel space limited their use to two-dimensional (2D) slices in which consistency across slices is not modeled explicitly. Concurrently with the present work, Wang et al. (2026) demonstrated tractable volumetric diffusion by operating in a latent space obtained by transfer from a frozen video autoencoder pretrained on natural images. Diffusion in a latent space learned on dose distributions themselves, rather than transferred, has to our knowledge not been investigated. Whether deterministic or generative with fixed sampling, these methods return a single dose distribution for a given anatomy, and therefore commit to a specific set of choices in clinical trade-offs learned during training. In clinical practice, treatment planning requires balancing competing constraints with preferences and protocols varying across clinicians and institutions. The lack of efficient human-in-the-loop control has been identified as a challenge to the clinical integration of ATP ( Gao et al., 2025a ) . Two recent frameworks make these trade-offs adjustable. Gao et al. (2025a) introduce a preference penalty within a GAN-based framework, and Wang et al. (2026) align predictions to institutional preferences through reinforcement learning post-training. In both cases, the preference specification must be integrated into the training procedure in a supervised way, and Any2Any further assumes fixed planning preferences per institution, which is not verified clinically ( Nelms et al., 2012 ) . A second obstacle to the use of such models in clinics is how they are typically evaluated. Performance is almost always reported as the voxel-wise agreement with a single reference plan, together with dose-volume histogram (DVH)-derived error ( Babier et al., 2021 ) . These quantities measure the reproduction of one acceptable plan among the many possibilities rather than the clinical acceptability of the prediction. They are computed on grids, crops and normalizations that differ between studies, making inter-study direct comparisons difficult ( Kui et al., 2024 ; Zamanian et al., 2025 ) . Additionally, accuracy measured on the predicted dose does not guarantee the clinical acceptability of the plan generated from it. In their OpenKBP-Opt study, Babier et al. (2022) report a moderate positive correlation (Spearman, ρ \rho between 0.5 and 0.62) between dose prediction performance and plan quality; a model outperforming another one on dose prediction metrics will not always yield a better plan. Conventional dose prediction evaluation metrics are therefore necessary but insufficient evidence of the clinical acceptability of the plan that is ultimately delivered, which is rarely evaluated or reported. In this work, we use a cohort of 900 clinically delivered volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) plans coming from five centers in three countries, spanning a range of prescription levels, protocols and planning styles. The dataset retains the inter-institutional and inter-clinician variability which is removed by construction when using a dataset of plans generated by a single automated treatment planning solution as is the case in the public AAPM GDP-HMM cohort ( Gao et al., 2025b ) . Nonetheless, we also report results on this dataset to provide a benchmark against which future work can be compared directly. We introduce LaDose , a radiotherapy-specific latent diffusion framework for fully 3D dose prediction, trained on 900 clinically delivered plans from five centers in three countries. In a six-framework comparison on this cohort, LaDose is the only model without a statistically significant bias across dosimetric endpoints, and the first latent diffusion predictor evaluated in a blinded expert review. It systematically addresses three core challenges: the representation in which generation occurs, the injection and control of clinical intent, and the clinical validity of the resulting plans. Our contributions are as follows: 1. A dose-specific latent space for whole-volume generation. We learn a latent space that captures the manifold of physically and clinically plausible dose maps. Because a dose distribution is a smooth field constrained by the physics of delivery, this manifold admits aggressive compression—reaching a factor of 128, compared with 16 for the dose latent space of concurrent work ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Generation therefore proceeds on entire volumes on a single GPU, without spatial decomposition and without loss of global consistency. The framework overcomes the scalability limits of conventional diffusion approaches while embedding prior knowledge of valid dose distributions. This relieves the denoiser of the need to learn what a plausible dose distribution looks like, freeing its capacity for the conditioning-to-dose mapping. 2. A generation-aware latent geometry. Latent diffusion pipelines typically optimize the autoencoder solely for reconstruction, leaving the geometry of the latent space unconstrained away from the encoder outputs—precisely the region occupied by sampled latents. We instead adapt latent denoising regularization ( Yang et al., 2026 ) to dose distributions, exposing the autoencoder to the same denoising objective used by the downstream diffusion model. The resulting latent space keeps perturbed latents decodable to valid dose distributions, so that residual denoiser error manifests as small, physically plausible deviations in voxel space. This incurs a measurable cost in voxel-wise reconstruction fidelity (a quantity never queried at inference) and yields a substantial gain in the quality of the predicted doses. 3. Disentangled conditioning. We separate target geometry from prescription information. Prescribed dose levels are supplied as exact scalar values rather than being painted into the voxel grid, where resampling, interpolation, and latent compression would otherwise degrade them. 4. Multiscale classifier-free guidance. We introduce a guidance mechanism that modulates the influence of each conditioning signal at inference time. This enables prescription-level and planner-level control over the generated plan and accommodates inter-institutional planning diversity without per-institution retraining or additional supervised training. 5. Evaluation on deliverable plans. We integrate the predictor with a dose-mimicking direct aperture optimization engine and report deliverable plan quality against the corresponding clinical plans for 30 patients treated from 2020 onwards, ensuring the comparison reflects current clinical practice. Acceptability is further assessed in a blinded review by three senior radiation oncologists and one senior medical physicist across three countries. The remainder of this work is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on automated treatment planning, deep-learning-based dose prediction and generalization across institutions, especially in the head-and-neck (HN) region. Section 3 describes the proposed radiotherapy-specific latent representation, the associated 3D diffusion-based dose prediction model and its integration with a fully automated treatment planning pipeline. Section 4 details the dataset, implementation details, and the evaluation framework. Section 5 reports reconstruction and prediction performance, along with the clinical acceptability of the generated plans. Section 6 discusses the design choices, the scope of the clinical evaluation and the directions for future work. 2 Related Work 2.1 Automated Treatment Planning and Dose Mimicking Knowledge-based planning (KBP) refers to the use of previously accepted and delivered plans to estimate an achievable dose distribution given a new anatomy. Initial KBP methods relied on geometric descriptors of the patient anatomy and PTV distribution ( Wu et al., 2009 ) to infer organ-wise DVHs ( Appenzoller et al., 2012 ) . The latter were then used as objectives for treatment planning systems (TPS). This approach brought improvements in terms of plan consistency and quality, and was adopted commercially ( Hansen et al., 2016 ) . However, a DVH is a one-dimensional summary of a three-dimensional dose distribution which, by nature, does not encode spatial information; two identical DVHs can mask substantial differences in hot spot and gradient location. Because the prediction of the complete dose distribution removes this ambiguity, it has become the preferred formulation in current ATP pipelines ( Babier et al., 2022 ) . Indeed, it provides an achievable voxel-wise objective for machine parameter optimization without requiring a clinician to specify them ( McIntosh et al., 2017 ) . 2.2 From Regression to Generative Dose Prediction Most existing frameworks formulate dose prediction as a deterministic voxel-wise regression task from CT; such approaches predominantly leverage U-Net-based architectures and their variants ( Kontaxis et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2021 ) , e.g., augmented with transformer components ( Hu et al., 2023 ) . Fully transformer-based architectures have been explored ( Wen et al., 2023 ) but are often limited to two-dimensional settings due to their high computational cost, a limitation that can be alleviated through latent-space compression of the input data ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Despite their success, regression-based methods are known to suffer from high-frequency detail loss ( Feng et al., 2023 ) and fail to integrate prior knowledge on the clinical and physical properties of valid dose distributions ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . This has led recent studies to formulate dose prediction as a generative modeling task. Approaches based on GANs ( Zhan et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) demonstrated improved local detail reconstruction, but are prone to unstable training and mode collapse ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) . Diffusion models (DMs) have shown superior performance in recovering high frequency details, leading to their adoption in dose prediction pipelines ( Feng et al., 2023 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) . However, the computational cost of diffusion models in voxel space has confined most work to a slice-wise formulation. Concurrently with the present work, Wang et al. (2026) achieved fully volumetric diffusion-based dose prediction by operating in a latent space with a compression rate of 16. They leverage a frozen video autoencoder pretrained on natural images (Wan 2.1, 127 M parameters). 2.3 Conditioning Signals The most common setting conditions on the planning CT, together with the PTV and OAR contours ( Liu et al., 2021 ; Nguyen et al., 2019 ; Gronberg et al., 2021 ) . Other models also supply geometric descriptors derived from the masks, in the form of signed distance maps, based on the hypothesis that the distance to the target boundary is a strong predictor of the dose distribution ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . A third family of approaches leverages the geometry of the delivered plan. Teng et al. (2024) generate binary beam masks to allow for downstream beam-wise decomposition and refinement of the predicted dose. The publicly available GDP-HMM dataset ( Gao et al., 2025b ) provides beam plates and an additional input modality, encoding delivery geometry ( Xiong et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Cao et al. (2025) combine beam trajectories with pencil-beam dose calculation to ground the prediction in the physics of the delivery. Reconstruction performance improves with this conditioning strength progression, along with the preprocessing burden. The handling of the prescription condition is largely inherited from the dataset on which each method is developed. The OpenKBP dataset ( Babier et al., 2021 ) contains a single prescription protocol (70/63/56 Gy). Associated released implementations commonly encode prescription by assigning the prescribed dose to the associated PTV contour ( Liu et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Uniform prescription protocols render the prescription condition uninformative and absorb it into the constant dose normalization ( Fu et al., 2024 ) . The GDP-HMM dataset ( Gao et al., 2025b ) contains multiple prescription protocols, and the prescription is encoded by assigning the prescribed dose to the associated PTV contour ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . When supplied, the prescribed dose is carried by a spatial input and undergoes the same resampling, interpolation and compression in the case of a latent formulation ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . 2.4 Clinical Preference Integration Two recent frameworks allow for the integration of clinical preferences. Gao et al. (2025a) introduce a homogeneity index and per OAR sliders, which can be manually tuned at inference time by the user to adjust OAR sparing or target coverage. To do so, they sample slider values during training and add a secondary supervised objective in the loss function of the model, which correlates slider values to dosimetric endpoints. Wang et al. (2026) align their dose prediction model to specific institutes via an additional reinforcement learning step, which requires retraining the model for each new institution. 2.5 Generalization Across Institutions and Protocols Historically, dose prediction frameworks have been trained and evaluated on single-center cohorts of anatomical sites such as lung or prostate, or on intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) delivery. In an effort to enable generalization, the GDP-HMM challenge released a large dataset of IMRT and VMAT plans for multiple prescription protocols across the head-and-neck and thoracic regions ( Gao et al., 2025b ) . The plans are, however, generated automatically and thus follow a single, consistent planning style. The authors report that they have not been clinically approved at this stage. Due to the high density of critical anatomical structures and the use of VMAT as the predominant delivery mode ( Alfouzan, 2021 ) , accurate dose delivery is particularly challenging in the HN region ( Zamanian et al., 2025 ) . Moreover, heterogeneous evaluation practices and limited data availability further complicate progress in HN dose prediction ( Kui et al., 2024 ) . 3 Methods 3.1 Preliminaries Diffusion Models Diffusion models generate samples by learning to reverse a stochastic corruption process. VMAT Delivery and Treatment Planning External beam radiotherapy delivers ionizing radiation to the patient using a linear accelerator (LINAC). The LINAC gantry rotates around the patient, while the photon beam is shaped by a multi-leaf collimator (MLC) consisting of opposing rows of motorized tungsten leaves. The delivered radiation is quantified in monitor units (MU). In VMAT, gantry rotation, MLC leaf positions, and dose rate vary continuously and simultaneously ( Alfouzan, 2021 ) . For treatment planning, delivery is discretized into control points, each defining the gantry angle, dose rate, and MLC aperture. Inverse planning determines a sequence of control points whose accumulated dose achieves adequate target coverage while satisfying the clinical constraints imposed by neighboring OARs. 3.2 Radiotherapy-Specific 3D Latent Representation Diffusion directly in voxel space is computationally prohibitive at the resolution of clinical dose distributions and therefore requires a compact latent representation ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . The choice of latent space determines both the computational cost of diffusion and the complexity of the distribution that the denoising network must model. We therefore learn a radiotherapy-specific latent space directly from dose distributions rather than adopting a general-purpose latent representation designed for natural images. We use variational autoencoders (VAEs) to encode the different input modalities into compact volumetric representations. The diffusion process is performed entirely in the latent space, while a dedicated dose decoder maps generated dose latents back to voxel space. Because dose distributions are smooth scalar fields governed by the physics of radiation delivery, their intrinsic dimensionality is substantially lower than that of natural images. A dose-specific latent space can therefore exploit this structure to achieve high compression while retaining the spatial detail required for accurate dose prediction. In addition, the dose decoder implicitly captures the prior of plausible dose distributions, allowing the diffusion model to focus primarily on learning the conditional mapping from patient and treatment information to dose. This creates a potential mismatch between training and inference: the decoder is trained primarily on z 0 z_{0} , the latent representations produced by the encoder, whereas during diffusion sampling it receives z ^ 0 \hat{z}_{0} , an estimate of the clean latent obtained after a finite number of denoising steps. If the decoder is poorly behaved in this neighborhood, small denoising errors can result in disproportionately large reconstruction errors in voxel space.
